content: Triage is a critical process in emergency medical care that allows first-responding personnel to allocate limited resources effectively and provide immediate care to victims until additional help arrives. The use of triage tags facilitates this process by enabling responders to quickly identify and prioritize patients based on the severity of their injuries. This concept was first introduced by Baron Dominique Jean Larrey, a French surgeon in Napoleon’s army. The START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) method is a widely used strategy by first responders and medical personnel to assess the severity of injuries in victims within 30 to 60 seconds. Triage tags are placed near the victim’s head to ensure clear visibility, allowing subsequent responders to easily identify and address the most critical cases when they arrive. Triage tags are typically two-sided, but their design varies between states and governmental agencies. While there is no universal standard for triage tag design, they are now commonly used to improve the management of victims during emergencies. Each state has implemented its own version of triage tags to meet specific needs. One popular type of triage tag is the Smart Tag, which features a unique folded design. This design allows for quick and efficient triage while enabling the tag to be updated without replacement, facilitating re-triage as a patient’s condition changes. The Smart Tag has been adopted as the standard triage tag in New York, Connecticut, Philadelphia, Boston, and Nevada. The basic sections of a triage tag include the following: Four color-coded categories: Black (Deceased): No care required. Red (Immediate): Life-threatening injuries requiring urgent care. Yellow (Delayed): Non-life-threatening injuries that can wait for treatment. Green (Minor): Minor injuries requiring minimal care. A section for vital signs and treatment information: This includes details such as the patient’s gender, residential address, medical history, and any administered treatments. A pictorial representation of the human body: Medical personnel can mark injured areas on the diagram for clarity. Triage tags are divided into three main categories: 1. Tear-off sections to label the victim’s injury severity and inform other medical personnel of their status. 2. A main body section for first responders to document their assessment, which remains with the patient. 3. Peel-off stickers to record transportation or treatment details provided to the victim. The use of triage tags offers several benefits. In addition to improving traffic flow and distributing care among injured patients, they facilitate the collection of critical data. Information can be added to the tag throughout the triage process, and in cases where a patient’s condition changes, the tag can be updated or replaced as needed. Some tags, such as the Smart Tag, allow for priority adjustments without requiring a new tag, streamlining the process. Examples of triage tag designs include: The MT-137 design, used by the military and various federal, state, and local agencies. The Smart Tag, developed by TSG Associates in the UK, which has been adopted by New York (2004), the British Military (2002), the London Ambulance Service during the 2005 terrorist bombings, and combined forces in Afghanistan (2006). The older Cruciform card, used in parts of the UK, including the North Sea oil industry and the Royal London Hospital during the 2005 London bombings. Different states and organizations have adopted customized designs to suit their needs. For example: Maryland and New Jersey use more detailed, customized triage tag designs. Community Emergency Response Teams (CERT) often carry color-coded flagging tape for triage purposes. Connecticut and Massachusetts have mandated the use of the Smart Tag statewide. The implementation of triage tags, particularly those with dynamic and adaptable designs, has significantly improved the efficiency and accuracy of emergency medical response systems.
